metadata.title: Indiscipline: The school climate of Brazilian schools and the impact on student performance

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2018 microdata for Brazil (15-year-olds) and constructs a disciplinary/school climate index from student questionnaire items. The analytic sample is restricted to students with complete data on all variables used in matching, and schools without teachers are removed as an outlier/invalid case. The manuscript does not report applying PISA sampling weights or any replicate-weight variance estimation; therefore, the results should be interpreted as estimates from the selected sample rather than fully design-weighted population parameters. Because the identification strategy is propensity score matching and dose-response estimation (not ML prediction), the paper’s weighting approach is not documented; analysts using the PISA database should consider whether to apply the official student sampling weights (and replicate weights if available) for variance estimation.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Uses PISA 2018 for Brazil (15-year-olds). The disciplinary climate index is built from five student-reported frequency items in language-of-instruction classes; students are grouped into treatment (negative climate) vs control (positive climate) based on whether the PISA disciplinary climate index is below/above zero (relative to the OECD mean). Schools that declared having no teachers are removed. The final analytic sample keeps only observations with no missing values in any variable used in the matching/estimation; sensitivity tests are mentioned for alternative indices (bullying and sense of belonging) but these were removed because they had many missings and would substantially reduce the sample.

main_findings.performance_metrics: PSM (nearest neighbor): -14.88 points (n=1), -12.7 (n=3), -11.95 (n=5); Kernel: -13.08; Radius: -13.2; IPWRA: -13.37. OLS with school fixed effects: -8 points. DRF: -9.06 points (dose-response).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Grade 10+ Reading data for Brazil, the study leveraged Disciplinary climate index (climate_test), socioeconomic status (escs), teacher support (teacher_support), sense of belonging (feel_belongging), and peers like me (like_me) to estimate the effect of negative school climate on reading grade, finding that negative school climate reduced reading scores by about 12–15 points depending on the matching estimator (and by 8 points under OLS with school fixed effects). This indicates that improving classroom disciplinary climate—especially reducing frequent disruptions in language-of-instruction classes—may raise reading achievement, though the design is observational and reverse causality cannot be ruled out.

main_findings.performance_metrics: PSM (nearest neighbor): -15.33 points (n=1), -12.34 (n=3), -11.9 (n=5); Kernel: -12.22; Radius: -12.3; IPWRA: -12.64. OLS with school fixed effects: -7 points. DRF: -8.3 points (dose-response).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Grade 10+ Mathematics data for Brazil, the study leveraged Disciplinary climate index (climate_test), socioeconomic status (escs), teacher support (teacher_support), grade repetition (grade_retention), and class size (size_class) to estimate the effect of negative school climate on math grade, finding that negative school climate reduced math scores by about 12–15 points across matching estimators (and by 7 points under OLS with school fixed effects). This indicates that policies targeting classroom order and reduced interruptions may improve mathematics performance, while the causal interpretation remains limited by observational selection and the possibility that low achievement contributes to disorder.

main_findings.performance_metrics: PSM (nearest neighbor): -13.2 points (n=1), -10.05 (n=3), -9.44 (n=5); Kernel: -10.42; Radius: -10.5; IPWRA: -10.59. OLS with school fixed effects: -5 points. DRF: -6.72 points (dose-response).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Grade 10+ Science data for Brazil, the study leveraged Disciplinary climate index (climate_test), socioeconomic status (escs), teacher support (teacher_support), teacher experience (years_teacher), and sense of belonging (feel_belongging) to estimate the effect of negative school climate on science grade, finding that negative school climate reduced science scores by roughly 10–13 points under matching (and by 5 points under OLS with school fixed effects). This indicates that strengthening disciplinary climate in school can support science learning outcomes, though the study’s observational matching framework cannot fully eliminate unobserved confounding or reverse causality.

data.outcome_summary: The paper analyzes PISA 2018 for Brazil (15-year-olds) and defines a disciplinary/school climate index from five student questionnaire items about classroom disruptions in language-of-instruction classes. Students are classified into negative vs positive climate groups, and the study estimates the effect on PISA reading, mathematics, and science scale scores using propensity score matching (nearest neighbor with replacement, plus Kernel and Radius), inverse probability-weighted regression adjustment (IPWRA), and robustness checks including Rosenbaum bounds and an OLS model with school fixed effects. Across matching methods, negative school climate is associated with lower achievement by about 12–15 points in math/reading and about 10–13 points in science; the dose-response function shows smaller but still negative effects (e.g., reading −9.06, math −8.3, science −6.72). The analysis uses complete cases only and does not document the use of PISA sampling/replicate weights, and the authors acknowledge potential reverse causality between climate and performance.
